anchorData: All figures are ILLUSTRATIVE (a made-up classroom example) unless marked as a standard value. SHELF ITEMS (6): lemon juice, vinegar, wood ash, baking soda, antacid tablet, tin of cooking salt. Extra items tested in Lesson 2: orange juice, soda drink, tap water, liquid bleach (diluted, teacher-handled), washing soda solution. UNIVERSAL INDICATOR (UI) colours and pH (standard simplified chart): red pH 0-2 (strong acid); orange/yellow pH 3-6 (weak acid); green pH 7 (neutral); blue pH 8-11 (weak base); purple/violet pH 12-14 (strong base). CLASS TEST TABLE (pH is an approximate classroom reading, to the nearest whole number): lemon juice pH 2 red, acidic; vinegar pH 3 orange-red, acidic; orange juice pH 4 orange, acidic; soda drink pH 3 orange, acidic; tap water pH 7 green, neutral; baking soda solution pH 8 blue-green, weakly basic; antacid tablet in water pH 9 blue, basic; wood ash solution pH 12 purple, strongly basic (ash filtrate); washing soda solution pH 11 blue-purple, basic; diluted bleach pH 11 blue-purple, basic (teacher demo only); cooking salt solution pH 7 green, neutral. STOMACH: stomach juice contains hydrochloric acid, pH about 2 (standard value, approximate). Heartburn = stomach acid pushed up into the food pipe (oesophagus). Antacid in the story contains a base/carbonate; the class model uses magnesium hydroxide as the base example. REACTIONS (word equations only, symbol equations optional but must be balanced): acid + base -> salt + water (hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide -> sodium chloride + water; hydrochloric acid + magnesium hydroxide -> magnesium chloride + water). Acid + carbonate -> salt + water + carbon dioxide (ethanoic acid [vinegar] + sodium hydrogencarbonate [baking soda] -> sodium ethanoate + water + carbon dioxide). Acid + metal -> salt + hydrogen (dilute hydrochloric acid + magnesium -> magnesium chloride + hydrogen). Gas tests: CO2 turns limewater milky; hydrogen gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint. Neutralisation practical: 10 cm3 of 0.1 M dilute HCl in a beaker with UI turns from red to green when dilute NaOH of the same strength is added dropwise until 10 cm3 has been added (illustrative, 1:1 ratio of equal molarity). AIR EXPOSURE (illustrative class results after leaving 2 g samples in open watch glasses for 3 days; mass change stated): cooking salt (humid rainy-day air, Mombasa) +0.3 g, becomes damp and clumpy (hygroscopic, with small impurities such as magnesium chloride; pure NaCl only slightly hygroscopic); anhydrous calcium chloride +3.0 g, dissolves into liquid (deliquescent); washing soda crystals (sodium carbonate decahydrate) -1.2 g, crumble to white powder (efflorescent); dry table sugar/sand control 0.0 g no change. Check: 2.0+0.3=2.3 g; 2.0+3.0=5.0 g; 2.0-1.2=0.8 g. Definitions: hygroscopic = takes in water vapour from air without necessarily dissolving; deliquescent = takes in so much water vapour that it dissolves and forms a solution; efflorescent = loses water of crystallisation to the air and crumbles to powder. SALT USES (Lesson 7, general facts, no numbers): agriculture (NPK fertilisers e.g. ammonium nitrate, calcium ammonium nitrate, and gypsum/lime), food (preservation of fish and meat, flavour), medicine (oral rehydration salts, Epsom salt magnesium sulfate, antacids), laundry (washing soda, sodium carbonate water softening), roads (salt used to melt ice in cold countries, NOT needed in Kenya's climate; calcium chloride used to settle dust on murram roads). ENVIRONMENT: eutrophication = excess nitrate and phosphate from fertiliser run-off into Lake Victoria causes algae and water hyacinth growth, oxygen depletion and fish death; soil pollution = over-salting/ acidification of soil; air pollution = ammonium and nitrogen oxide compounds from fertiliser use, sulfur dioxide forms acid rain. SALT AND HEALTH: WHO recommends less than 5 g salt per day (about 1 level teaspoon) for adults (standard figure, 5 g = 2 g sodium). Class illustration: a plate of ugali with sukuma wiki seasoned with 1 teaspoon (5 g) salt, nyama choma, and a packet of crisps; a made-up family daily salt total of 12 g from table salt 6 g + stock cube 2 g + salted fish/nyama 3 g + crisps 1 g = 12 g, which is 7 g above the 5 g limit (12-5=7; 12/5=2.4 times the limit). Excess salt raises blood volume and blood pressure (simplified).
characters: Mama Amina: Mombasa home cook who keeps lemon juice, vinegar, wood ash, baking soda, an antacid tablet and a tin of cooking salt on her kitchen shelf. Her son (named Juma): has heartburn after a spicy meal; antacid helps; the doctor advises the family to reduce salt. The doctor (Dr. Wanjiru, at a Mombasa clinic): warns about salt and blood pressure; says the antacid neutralises excess stomach acid. Mombasa: humid coastal town, damp salt tin in rainy season. Washing soda bag: left open on a dry day, crumbles (efflorescence). Mr. Otieno: Kisumu fish trader who salts fish to preserve it (Lesson 7). Farmer Kiprop: Kericho tea farmer using fertiliser; run-off concern (Lesson 7). Lake Victoria: eutrophication and water hyacinth example. Class: Grade 10 learners in groups of 4; the teacher is called Teacher. Class model: a poster titled 'The Mombasa Kitchen Model' revised in every lesson. DQB: Driving Question Board with sticky notes.
outcome: The substances behave differently because of their chemistry. Acids (lemon juice, vinegar) release hydrogen ions in water and turn universal indicator red or orange; bases (wood ash, antacid) release hydroxide ions and turn it blue or purple. Vinegar fizzes on baking soda and an antacid fizzes in water because an acid reacts with a carbonate to make a salt, water and carbon dioxide gas. An antacid relieves Juma's heartburn by neutralising excess stomach acid, forming a salt and water. Salt in the open tin gets damp because it is hygroscopic in humid Mombasa air, while washing soda crumbles because it loses water of crystallisation. Salts are useful (food, farming, medicine, laundry) but excess salt in food raises blood pressure and excess fertiliser salts harm lakes, so use must be proper and in the right amount.
conventions: Use 'hydrogen ions (H+)' for acids and 'hydroxide ions (OH-)' for bases; limit the definition to this (no Bronsted-Lowry or Lewis). pH scale 0-14; below 7 acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic (alkaline). Use 'base' for any substance that neutralises acids and 'alkali' for a base dissolved in water; wood ash solution is an alkali. Use 'universal indicator' and 'pH chart' with the colours in anchorData. Use 'baking soda (sodium hydrogencarbonate)' and 'washing soda (sodium carbonate)' consistently and treat both as carbonate-type bases for reaction purposes. Say 'neutralisation' for acid + base -> salt + water. Use 'dilute' for acids and bases in practicals (about 0.1 M). Chemical names: hydrochloric acid, ethanoic acid (vinegar, about 5% ethanoic acid), sodium chloride (cooking salt). Salt behaviours: hygroscopic, deliquescent, efflorescent exactly as defined in anchorData. Units: grams (g), cm3, pH has no unit, mass change shown with + or -. Safety: goggles, never taste lab chemicals, wash splashes with plenty of water, bleach handled by teacher only, no naked flames near hydrogen except a small test splint by the teacher. 40-minute lessons; phase minutes must add to 40. KICD values and competencies copied verbatim from the sub-strand. All data are illustrative unless marked standard. Do not claim cooking salt is strongly hygroscopic; use the impurity explanation. Heartburn is not related to the heart.
